When you see the abomination

But when you see the abomination that brings ruin standing where he has no right to be (let the reader take note), then those who are in Judea must escape to the hills. Anyone who is on the roof must not go down into the house to fetch anything out of it. Anyone who is out in the field must not go back for a cloak. How terrible it will be in those days for women who are expecting a child or nursing a baby! Pray that this does not come in winter. For those days will bring distress unlike any there has been from the beginning, when God created the world, until now, or ever will be again. If the Lord had not cut those days short, no one at all would survive. But because of the chosen, those he chose for himself, he has cut the days short. At that time, if anyone tells you, ‘See, here is the Christ!’ or ‘See, there he is!’ do not believe it. For false christs and false prophets will rise up and do signs and wonders, so as to lead the chosen ones astray, if that could be done. So you must be on your guard. I have told you all of it in advance.

The Son of Man coming in the clouds

But in those days, after that time of distress, the sun will grow dark and the moon will give no light. Stars will come falling from the sky, and the powers in the heavens will be shaken. Then people will see the Son of Man come in clouds, with great power and glory. And then he will send out the angels and gather the chosen ones from all four winds, from the farthest edge of the earth to the farthest edge of the sky.

Learn from the fig tree

Learn this parable from the fig tree. Once its branch turns soft and its leaves sprout, you know summer is close. So too with you: when you see these things happening, be sure that it is near, right at the door. Truly I tell you, this generation will certainly not pass away before all these things take place. Heaven and earth will pass away, yet my words will never pass away.

Keep awake

As for that day or hour, nobody knows it, neither the angels in heaven nor the Son. Only the Father knows. Be on your guard and stay alert, because you do not know when the time will come. It is like a man who goes away from home. He leaves his house, puts his servants in charge, each with a task to do, and orders the doorkeeper to keep watch. So keep watch, since you cannot know when the master of the house is coming: in the evening, at midnight, at the crowing of the rooster, or at dawn. Otherwise he may arrive suddenly and find you asleep. What I tell you, I tell everyone: Keep watch!”

fields.title: Mark 14
fields.body_html:
A plot two days before the Passover

Two days remained before the Passover and the Feast of Unleavened Bread. The chief priests and the scribes were looking for a way to take him by a trick and put him to death. For they kept saying, “Not at the feast, in case the people raise an uproar.”

Anointed at Bethany

Jesus was in Bethany, at the home of Simon the leper. While he lay at the meal, a woman came with an alabaster flask of pure nard, a perfumed oil of great value. She broke the flask and poured the oil over his head. Some of those present were angry and said to one another, “What is the point of wasting this perfume? It could have fetched more than a year’s wages, and the money could have gone to the poor.” So they turned on her with harsh words. But Jesus said, “Let her be. Why are you bothering her? She has done a beautiful thing for me. The poor will be with you at all times, and you can help them any time you wish. But you will not always have me. She did what was in her power. She has poured perfume on my body ahead of time, to make it ready for burial. Truly I tell you, in every place in the whole world where the gospel is proclaimed, people will tell what she has done, and remember her.”

Judas goes to the chief priests

Then one of the Twelve, Judas Iscariot, went off to the chief priests to betray him to them. They were delighted to hear it and promised to pay him. So Judas looked for a good chance to betray him.

Preparing the Passover

On the first day of Unleavened Bread, the day the Passover lambs were sacrificed, his disciples said to him, “Where would you like us to go and make ready for you to eat the Passover meal?” So he sent off two of his disciples with these instructions: “Go into the city. A man carrying a water jar will come to meet you. Follow him, and when he goes into a house, tell the owner of the house, ‘The Teacher says, “Which is my guest room, where I am to eat the Passover with my disciples?”‘ He himself will show you a big upper room, set out with couches and ready. Get things ready for us there.” So the disciples set out, came into the city and found it all as he had said, and there they prepared the Passover.

One of you will hand me over

When evening came, he arrived with the Twelve. As they lay at the table and ate, Jesus told them, “Truly I tell you, one of you here, eating with me, will betray me.” They were deeply hurt, and one after another they said to him, “It is not I, is it?” He said to them, “It is one of the Twelve, one who dips bread into the bowl with me. The Son of Man is going as it stands written about him, but how terrible for the man who betrays the Son of Man! It would be good for that man if he had never been born.”

My body, my blood of the covenant

During the meal he took bread, spoke the blessing, broke it and handed it to them, saying, “Take it. This is my body.” He also took a cup, and after giving thanks he passed it to them, and every one of them drank from it. He said to them, “This is my blood of the covenant, poured out for many. Truly I tell you, I will never again drink the fruit of the vine until the day I drink it new in the kingdom of God.”

Then they sang a hymn and went out to the Mount of Olives.

Peter’s denial foretold

Jesus told them, “All of you will stumble and fall away, for it stands written, ‘I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered.’ But after I am raised up, I will lead the way ahead of you into Galilee.” Peter told him, “They may all fall away, but I will not.” Jesus answered him, “Truly I tell you, before a rooster crows twice today, this very night, you yourself will deny me three times.” But Peter kept saying all the more firmly, “Should I have to die with you, still I will never deny you.” And every one of them said the same.

Gethsemane

Then they came to a place by the name of Gethsemane, and he said to his disciples, “Stay seated here while I pray.” He took Peter, James and John with him, and horror and anguish came over him. He said to them, “My soul is filled with grief, grief enough to die. Wait here and stay awake.” He went on a little way, threw himself to the ground and prayed that the hour might pass him by, if that could be. He said, “Abba, Father, for you all things are possible. Remove this cup from me. Yet let it be what you will, not what I will.” Then he came back and found them asleep. He said to Peter, “Simon, are you asleep? Did you not have the strength to stay awake a single hour? Stay awake and pray that you will not come into temptation. The spirit is eager, but the flesh is weak.” He went away again and prayed, using the same words. Coming back again, he found them asleep; they could not keep their eyes open, and they had no answer to give him. He came a third time and said to them, “Still asleep? Still resting? Enough of that! The hour is here. See, the Son of Man is being handed over into the power of sinners. Get up; we must go. Look, the one who betrays me is near.”

Arrested with a kiss

Right then, as he was still talking, Judas came up, one of the Twelve. A crowd came with him carrying swords and clubs. They had been sent by the chief priests, the scribes and the elders. Judas, the betrayer, had given them a signal beforehand. “The one I kiss is him,” he had said. “Take hold of him and lead him away under close guard.” As soon as he arrived, he went straight up to Jesus and said, “Rabbi!” and kissed him. They then laid hands on him and took him prisoner. But one of the bystanders pulled out his sword, hit the high priest’s servant and cut off his ear. Jesus said to them, “Have you come with swords and clubs to seize me, as you would a bandit? Day after day I was among you in the temple, teaching, and you did not lay a hand on me. But this is happening so that the Scriptures would be fulfilled.” And they all left him and ran.

A certain young man had been going along with him, with only a linen sheet thrown around his bare body. They seized him, but he slipped out of the linen sheet and ran away naked.

Before the council

Jesus was led off to the high priest’s house, where all the chief priests, elders and scribes came together. Peter kept well back, but followed him all the way inside the high priest’s courtyard. He sat down among the guards and warmed himself by the firelight. Meanwhile the chief priests and the entire Council searched for testimony against Jesus that would let them have him executed, but they could not find any. Plenty of people testified falsely against him, but what they said did not match. Then some of them got up and brought a false charge against him: “We heard him declare, ‘I will pull down this temple that human hands have made, and in three days I will put up another that no hands have made.’” But even on this point what they said did not match. The high priest rose, stepped into the middle and put a question to Jesus: “Have you no answer at all? What is this that these people are saying against you?” But he kept silent and made no answer at all. Again the high priest put a question to him: “Are you Christ, the Son of the Blessed One?” Jesus said, “I am. And you will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of the Power, and coming with the clouds of heaven.” The high priest ripped his clothes. “What more do we need witnesses for? You heard the blasphemy for yourselves. What is your verdict?” Every one of them condemned him: he deserved to die. Some of them started spitting on him. They covered his face, punched him and taunted him: “Prophesy!” The guards, too, took charge of him and struck him with open hands.

Peter denies knowing him

Meanwhile Peter was below in the courtyard. One of the high priest’s servant girls came along, and when she noticed Peter warming himself, she studied his face and said, “You, too, were with the man from Nazareth, Jesus.” But Peter denied it: “I have no idea what you are talking about; I do not understand you.” Then he went out to the entrance, and a rooster crowed. The servant girl caught sight of him there and started saying again to the people standing around, “He is one of them.” Again he denied it. A little later the bystanders again said to Peter, “You really are one of them. You are from Galilee, after all; the way you talk gives you away.” Then he started calling curses down and swearing oaths: “This man you speak of, I do not know him.” At that moment a rooster crowed for the second time. Peter remembered what Jesus had told him: “Before a rooster crows twice, you will deny me three times.” Then Peter broke down in tears.

fields.title: Mark 15
fields.body_html:
Before Pilate

As soon as it was morning, the chief priests met with the elders, the scribes and the whole Council and reached a decision. They bound Jesus, led him off, and handed him over to Pilate. Pilate questioned him, “So you are the King of the Jews?” He answered him, “You have said so.” The chief priests kept bringing many charges against him. So Pilate put another question to him: “Have you no answer at all? Look at all the charges they are bringing against you.” But Jesus made no further reply at all, and Pilate was astonished.

At the festival it was his custom to set free for them one prisoner of their choosing. A man named Barabbas was in prison along with the rebels who had killed people in the uprising. The crowd came up and began to ask Pilate to do for them what he always did. Pilate replied, “Shall I set free the King of the Jews for you? Is that what you want?” Pilate could see that envy was what had moved the chief priests to hand him over to him. But the chief priests worked up the crowd to have him free Barabbas for them instead. Pilate spoke to them again. “Then what would you have me do with the man you call the King of the Jews?” They shouted back, “Crucify him!” Pilate asked them, “Why? What crime has he committed?” But they only shouted louder, “Crucify him!” So Pilate, wishing to please the crowd, freed Barabbas for them. He had Jesus flogged and then handed him over for crucifixion.

The soldiers mock the king

The soldiers took him into the palace courtyard, that is, the governor’s headquarters, and called the whole company of soldiers together. They put a purple robe on him, wove a crown out of thorny branches and put it on his head. Then they started saluting him: “Long live the King of the Jews!” Again and again they hit him on the head with a stick, spat on him, and went down on their knees to pay him homage. When they had finished mocking him, they stripped the purple robe off him and dressed him in his own clothes. Then they took him out to crucify him.

Crucified at Golgotha

A man named Simon from Cyrene was coming in from the countryside and passing by; he was the father of Alexander and Rufus. The soldiers pressed him into carrying the cross for Jesus. They brought Jesus to a place named Golgotha, meaning Place of a Skull. They tried to give him wine flavored with myrrh, but he would not take it. Then they crucified him. They shared out his clothes by throwing dice for them to see what each would get.

It was nine in the morning when they crucified him. The written charge against him said, “The King of the Jews.” They also crucified two bandits with him, one at his right and one at his left.

People who went by hurled insults at him, wagging their heads. “Ha!” they said. “So you were going to tear down the temple and raise it again in three days! Then save yourself by coming down from the cross!” The chief priests and the scribes mocked him in the same way among themselves. “He saved other people,” they said, “but he cannot save himself! Let Christ, the King of Israel, come down from the cross right now, so that we can see it and believe!” Even the men crucified with him heaped insults on him.

Darkness at noon and the torn curtain

At noon darkness fell over the whole land and lasted until three in the afternoon. At three o’clock Jesus gave a loud shout: “Eloi, Eloi, lema sabachthani?” That means, “My God, my God, why did you abandon me?” Some of the bystanders heard it and said, “Listen, he is calling for Elijah!” Someone ran and soaked a sponge in sour wine, put it on the end of a stick and offered it to him to drink. “Wait!” he said. “Let us see if Elijah will come and take him down.” But Jesus gave a loud cry and breathed his last. And the curtain in the sanctuary was split in two from top to bottom. The centurion standing in front of him saw how he died, and he said, “This man really was God’s Son!”

The women watching from a distance

Women were also there, looking on from far off, among them Mary Magdalene; Mary, mother of the younger James and of Joses; and Salome. In Galilee they had followed him and looked after his needs. Many other women were there as well, who had come with him up to Jerusalem.

Laid in a tomb cut from rock

Evening was already coming on. Since it was the day of Preparation, the day before the Sabbath, Joseph from Arimathea came. He was a respected member of the Council who was also looking for the kingdom of God. He boldly went in to Pilate and requested the body of Jesus. Pilate was surprised that he could already be dead. He called the centurion and asked him whether he had been dead for some time. When the centurion told him, he gave the body to Joseph. Joseph bought a linen cloth, took him down and wrapped him in it. He laid him in a tomb that had been carved out of the rock, and he rolled a stone over the entrance of the tomb. Mary Magdalene and Mary the mother of Joses were watching to see where he was placed.

fields.title: Mark 16
fields.body_html:
He has been raised

After the Sabbath had passed, Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James, and Salome purchased spices so that they could go and anoint his body. On the first day of the week, very early, when the sun had come up, they came to the tomb. They had been asking each other, “Who is going to roll the stone back from the entrance to the tomb for us?” When they looked up, they could see the stone had already been rolled away, and it was a huge stone. On entering the tomb they found a young man seated on the right, wearing a white robe, and they were stunned. But he told them, “Do not be alarmed. You have come looking for Jesus from Nazareth, the one who was crucified. He has been raised; he is not here. Look, this is the place where they laid him. But go and tell his disciples, and Peter too, that he is going on ahead of you to Galilee. You will see him there, as he said to you.” They went out and ran from the tomb, trembling and beside themselves. And they told no one anything, for they were afraid.

The shorter ending

The earliest manuscripts of Mark end at 16:8. The two endings that follow, a short one and the longer one in 16:9–20, were added later. Most Bibles print them, as here, set apart and in brackets.

[They gave Peter and those with him a short report of all they had been told. After this Jesus himself sent out through them, from east to west, the sacred and imperishable proclamation of eternal salvation. Amen.]

The longer ending: Jesus appears

[After he had risen, early in the morning of the first day of the week, he showed himself first to Mary Magdalene. It was from her that he had thrown out seven demons. She went and brought the news to the people who had been with him, who were grieving and weeping. But on hearing that he was alive and that she had seen him, they would not believe it.

After that he appeared to two of them in a different form, as they were walking along on their way into the country. These two went back and told the others, but they did not believe them either.

Later he appeared to the eleven themselves as they were eating. He rebuked them for their unbelief and their stubborn hearts, because they had not believed those who had seen him risen. He told them, “Go out into the whole world and announce the gospel to all of creation. Whoever has believed and been baptized will be saved; anyone who refuses to believe will be condemned. These signs will go with those who believe: they will throw out demons in my name and speak in new tongues; they will lift up snakes; if they swallow any deadly poison, it will do them no harm; they will put their hands on those who are sick, and the sick will get better.”

Taken up into heaven

So the Lord Jesus, when he had spoken to them, was taken up into heaven and took his seat at the right hand of God. And they went out and proclaimed the message everywhere. The Lord worked with them and confirmed the word by the signs that came with it.]

fields.title: Conclusion
fields.body_html:
But go and tell his disciples, and Peter too, that he is going on ahead of you to Galilee. You will see him there, as he said to you.”

— Mark 16:7

Mark’s Gospel ends at an empty tomb, with a message the women are too frightened to pass on. But the message itself is the last word Jesus has for his disciples, and it is full of grace. They abandoned him; Peter denied him. He is going ahead of them, back to Galilee, where it all began, and he will meet them there. The road goes on. And Peter, of all people, is named.

The question the book leaves with you

Mark began with a title: “The beginning of the gospel about Jesus Christ.” By the end it is clear that the whole book has been only the beginning. The rest of the story, the meeting in Galilee, the message carried to the ends of the earth, is left for the reader to know and, in a sense, to continue. Mark has told us that the gospel must first be proclaimed “to all the nations”, and that wherever it is proclaimed in the whole world, a woman’s act of love will be told. He does not tell us how. He leaves the women silent at the tomb, and the reader holding the news.

So the question Mark leaves is the one Jesus asked on the road to Caesarea Philippi:

“And you,” he asked them, “who do you say I am?”

— Mark 8:29

Peter gave the right answer and did not yet understand it. A Roman centurion gave it at the cross, after watching Jesus die. Mark wants his readers to answer as the centurion did, knowing what it costs: the Christ is the one who came to serve and to give his life as the ransom price for many, and to follow him is to take up a cross.

Where the book points

It points, first, to the cross, not as a defeat that the resurrection reverses but as the place where Jesus is most fully revealed. In Mark the glory of God is seen in a servant.

It points, second, to discipleship as a journey, not an arrival. The disciples in Mark are always on the road, usually behind, often confused. Bartimaeus, who could see nothing, ends by following Jesus along the road. That is what faith looks like in this book: not a perfect understanding, but a desperate cry for mercy, a cloak thrown off, and a man walking after Jesus toward Jerusalem. “I believe! Help my unbelief!” is as good a prayer as any disciple has prayed.

And it points to hope for those who fail. The book does not hide the disciples’ fear or Peter’s denial, because the church that first heard it, very likely in Rome in the years of persecution, knew what it was to be afraid and to fall. Mark tells them that the risen Jesus goes ahead of his frightened followers, and waits for them.

Where to go from here

Mark has long been the quiet Gospel, but some of the church’s finest preachers have found in its vivid scenes exactly the details that open a sermon. A few places to begin in this library:

  • On the man behind the book. Eusebius of Caesarea’s The Church History, whose third book preserves what Papias said about Mark and Peter; and Hurlbut’s Life of Christ for Young and Old, which tells the Gospel story as one connected narrative.
  • On the touch and the look of Jesus. Alexander Maclaren preached on Mark more vividly than almost anyone: Christ’s Touch (1:41), The Secret of Gladness (2:19), The Toiling Christ (4:36–38), The Power of Feeble Faith (5:25–28) and The Looks of Jesus (5:32).
  • On prayer. Jesus, Teacher of Prayer, whose chapter “Very Early in the Morning” follows Jesus out to pray long before daylight (1:35).
  • On faith. A. B. Simpson’s The Possibilities of Faith, on Jesus’s words to the father of the boy with an unclean spirit (9:23).
  • On giving. Andrew Murray’s Christ’s Estimate of Money, on the widow’s two small coins (12:41–44).
  • On the empty tomb. Martin Luther’s Of Christ’s Resurrection, on the women at the tomb (16:1–8); and, from the longer ending, Catherine Booth’s Aggressive Christianity (16:15).

You can also go the other way, from the text to the classics. Every reference to Mark in this library can be tapped to read the verse, and the Scripture pages gather, chapter by chapter, what the great writers of the church have said about each passage of this Gospel.

But the best next step may be to read Mark again, aloud and all at once, and then to turn to the other Gospels. Matthew and Luke both follow Mark’s outline closely, and you will see how each fills it out. Yet Mark’s plain, urgent telling has a power of its own. It ends by sending you back to the beginning, to Galilee, where Jesus first walked by the lake and called four fishermen, and where he still calls:

“Come and follow me.”

— Mark 1:17
